unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Calderrow Tannery Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that has operated for 9 years. It employs 36 workers and produces 420,000 square metres of finished leather each year, with sales revenue of $2.4 million. Tanning uses 1,850 tonnes of salt, lime and chromium compounds annually, and the waste effluent is discharged into the River Senn after basic settling only.

Downstream of the tannery, 14 licensed fishermen report catches down 40% since the plant opened, blaming chromium pollution for fish kills and tainted water. The Environment Agency warns that discharges exceed the legal limit by 35%, with daily fines of $3,000 from 1 March unless the firm installs a $480,000 effluent treatment plant. The directors must choose between treating the waste, relocating upriver, or appealing the ruling.

questions.question_text: Define 'pollution'.
questions.model_answer: Pollution is the release of harmful substances or waste into the natural environment, such as chemical effluent entering rivers or fumes entering the air, damaging ecosystems and human health. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Release of harmful substances or waste into the environment
Causes damage to ecosystems, people or the environment

questions.question_text: Explain two external costs created by Calderrow Tannery.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The effluent damages the river's fish stocks [k], because pollution from the tannery is blamed for catches falling 40% for 14 licensed fishermen who gain no benefit from the factory [app]. Reason 2: The discharges impose costs on the wider community [k], as they exceed the legal limit by 35%, risking daily fines of $3,000 and tainted water for riverside households [app].

knowledge_max_2: External costs fall on third parties not involved in production
Pollution imposes costs beyond the polluting business
application_max_2: Catches down 40% for 14 licensed fishermen downstream
Discharges 35% above the legal limit; $3,000 daily fines

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Calderrow Tannery if it installs the effluent treatment plant.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The plant requires a large immediate outlay [k], costing $480,000 which must be funded from cash reserves or borrowing, straining the company's finances [app], so less money remains for wages, hides and repairs in the short term [an]. Problem 2: Running the plant adds ongoing costs [k], since treating 1,850 tonnes of salt, lime and chromium waste each year means buying chemicals, power and monitoring equipment [app], pushing up the cost per square metre of leather and squeezing profit margins [an].

knowledge_max_2: Large capital outlay strains business finances
Running costs raise average production costs
application_max_2: $480,000 installation cost for the treatment plant
1,850 tonnes of salt, lime and chromium compounds treated each year
analysis_max_2: Less cash available for other spending in the short term
Higher unit costs squeeze profit margins

questions.question_text: Do you think Calderrow Tannery should install the $480,000 effluent treatment plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for installing the plant is that it brings the firm into legal compliance immediately [k], avoiding $3,000 daily fines from 1 March while protecting the $2.4 million annual revenue and the jobs of 36 workers [app], so the firm can keep trading while restoring its reputation with the 14 licensed fishermen affected by chromium pollution [an]. However, one argument against is the strain on cash flow [k], as a $480,000 cost is one-fifth of a year's revenue and must be paid before any benefit is seen [app], so appealing could delay payment, but the firm would keep risking fines and eventual closure of the River Senn site [an]. Overall, Calderrow Tannery should install the effluent treatment plant [eval], because fines of $3,000 a day would exceed $1 million in a year of breach, more than double the $480,000 capital cost, and compliance permanently eliminates the pollution problem [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Compliance avoids fines and protects trading
Large capital outlay strains cash flow
application_max_2: $480,000 cost equals one-fifth of $2.4 million annual revenue
$3,000 daily fines from 1 March; 36 workers and 14 licensed fishermen affected
analysis_max_2: Continued trading protects revenue, jobs and reputation
Appealing keeps fines and closure risk hanging over the business
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both installing the plant and appealing or delaying
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Bramblefold Poultry Farm is a family partnership in Country X keeping 17,000 laying hens across two barns for 6 years. It sells 5.1 million eggs a year to regional supermarkets, earning $890,000 in sales revenue with 9 full-time employees. The farm sits just 400 metres from Lower Ashby village, home to 1,150 residents.

Over the past 18 months the district council has received 26 written complaints about ammonia smells and flies in hot weather. Its survey found boundary ammonia levels averaging 0.09 parts per million, twice the recommended figure for homes. Bramblefold can install covered manure storage and a bio-filter system costing $65,000, or cut its flock to 12,000 hens, lowering output by 30% but reducing odour and improving bird welfare.

questions.question_text: Define 'external costs'.
questions.model_answer: External costs are the costs of a business or economic activity that fall on third parties not involved in the production or consumption of the good, such as pollution, noise or odour affecting people living nearby. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Costs falling on third parties not involved in the activity
Examples include pollution, noise or odour affecting residents

questions.question_text: Explain two external costs created by Bramblefold Poultry Farm.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Odour from the barns harms villagers' quality of life [k], because boundary ammonia levels average 0.09 parts per million, twice the recommended figure for homes 400 metres away [app]. Reason 2: The farm imposes disruption on the community [k], as shown by 26 written complaints about flies and smells received over the past 18 months [app].

knowledge_max_2: External costs affect third parties, such as residents, not the producer
Odour, ammonia and flies are examples of external costs
application_max_2: Boundary ammonia averaging 0.09 parts per million, twice the recommended figure
26 written complaints received over the past 18 months

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Bramblefold would face if it cut its flock to 12,000 hens.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Egg output and income would fall [k], as removing about 5,000 hens cuts production by roughly 30% from 5.1 million eggs, reducing supermarket supply and revenue from $890,000 [app], so the partners' drawings and cash flow would shrink [an]. Problem 2: Staffing becomes less efficient [k], because the same two barns and 9 employees would serve a flock 30% smaller [app], raising the average cost per egg and squeezing profit margins [an].

knowledge_max_2: Cutting output reduces revenue
Fixed resources spread over fewer units raise unit costs
application_max_2: Flock cut from 17,000 to 12,000 hens, lowering output by 30% from 5.1 million eggs
Two barns and 9 employees working for a smaller flock
analysis_max_2: Partners' income and cash flow fall
Average cost per egg rises, squeezing profit margins

questions.question_text: Do you think Bramblefold should install the $65,000 bio-filter system instead of reducing its flock to 12,000 hens? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for the bio-filter is that it removes the odour problem while keeping full production [k], so Bramblefold keeps 17,000 hens and its $890,000 revenue with its 9 employees [app], protecting contracts with regional supermarkets and farm profits [an]. However, one argument against is the cost [k], as $65,000 is a large outlay for a farm earning $890,000 a year, and the system needs regular maintenance to stay effective [app], and ammonia could still drift if wind spreads it beyond the bio-filters, so 26 complaints may not stop immediately [an]. Overall, Bramblefold should install the $65,000 bio-filter system [eval], because keeping production at 5.1 million eggs preserves revenue far above the installation cost, whereas cutting the flock by 30% would permanently shrink the business and risk supermarket contracts [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Bio-filter removes odour while retaining output
Large outlay plus maintenance burden for the farm
application_max_2: $65,000 cost versus $890,000 annual revenue and 5.1 million eggs
Cutting to 12,000 hens would lower output by 30%
analysis_max_2: Full output protects supermarket contracts and profits
Residual ammonia drift may not stop all complaints
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both installing the bio-filter and cutting the flock
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Estwick Brick Co is a private limited company in Country X producing 9 million clay bricks a year for housebuilders. It employs 74 workers, operates two kilns around the clock and has annual turnover of $3.7 million. The town of Estwick, 500 metres away, is home to 9,000 residents, many in homes downwind of the chimneys.

Local doctors have recorded 34 cases of childhood asthma near the plant in the last year, and Environment Agency tests show chimney particulates 45% above the legal limit. The Agency may fine the company $1,500 per day of breach, or order the oldest kiln shut down. The board can fit electrostatic filters for $210,000, switch to low-sulphur gas at an extra $28,000 a year, or appeal against the ruling.

questions.question_text: Define 'externalities'.
questions.model_answer: Externalities are the effects of producing or consuming a good on third parties not involved in the transaction; they may be negative, such as pollution, or positive, such as jobs created for the local community. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Effects on third parties not involved in the transaction
Can be negative external costs or positive external benefits

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the Environment Agency intervenes in Estwick Brick Co's operations.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To protect public health [k], since 34 cases of childhood asthma were recorded near the plant in the last year, linked to dust drifting over 500 metres into a town of 9,000 residents [app]. Reason 2: To enforce the law against pollution [k], because chimney particulates measured 45% above the legal limit, so fines of $1,500 per day are needed to force compliance [app].

knowledge_max_2: To protect public health from pollution
To enforce legal limits and standards
application_max_2: 34 cases of childhood asthma near the plant last year
Particulates 45% above the legal limit; fines of $1,500 per day

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on Estwick Brick Co of fitting the electrostatic filters costing $210,000.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Emissions fall and fines stop [k], as filters capture particulates so the output stays legal and the $1,500 daily fines are avoided [app], preventing penalties that could total over $540,000 a year [an]. Effect 2: A large short-term cost [k], as $210,000 must be spent immediately, equal to about 5.7% of annual turnover of $3.7 million [app], squeezing short-term cash flow and reducing profit for the year [an].

knowledge_max_2: Filters reduce emissions and end fines
Filters are a large one-off capital cost
application_max_2: Filters cost $210,000 and avoid $1,500 daily fines
$210,000 equals about 5.7% of $3.7 million turnover
analysis_max_2: Avoided fines could save over $540,000 a year
Short-term cash flow and profit are squeezed

questions.question_text: Do you think Estwick Brick Co should fit the $210,000 electrostatic filters? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for fitting the filters is that they solve the legal problem permanently [k], removing the 45% excess particulates and stopping $1,500 daily fines while keeping both kilns running for its 9 million bricks [app], protecting turnover of $3.7 million, the jobs of 74 workers and relations with Estwick's 9,000 residents [an]. However, one argument against is the immediate cost [k], since $210,000 equals roughly 5.7% of annual turnover and the firm could instead switch to low-sulphur gas at just $28,000 a year extra, preserving cash for expansion [app], although switching fuel may not capture the heavier particulates and would delay compliance [an]. Overall, Estwick Brick Co should fit the electrostatic filters [eval], because fines of $1,500 a day would exceed the $210,000 installation cost in 5 months of breach, making compliance cheaper and safer for its licence to operate [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Filters deliver permanent legal compliance
Upfront cost versus cheaper but partial gas switching
application_max_2: $210,000 filter cost versus $28,000 extra per year for gas
45% excess particulates; fines of $1,500 per day
analysis_max_2: Compliance protects turnover, jobs and community relations
Gas switching is cheaper but may not capture heavier particulates
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both fitting filters and switching fuel or appealing
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Kongwe Plantations Ltd is a private limited company in Country X growing oil palm across 2,600 hectares for 11 years. It employs 190 workers, produces 7,400 tonnes of crude palm oil a year and exports 80% of its output to food manufacturers, earning $4.6 million in export revenue. Palm oil appears in 3,000 everyday supermarket products across the region.

Satellite surveys by Earthwatch Alliance, an environmental pressure group, show 640 hectares of irreplaceable native forest were cleared in the last 4 years, releasing stored carbon and destroying habitat. Buyers in Country Y now demand certified sustainable palm oil; certification costs $85,000 a year, plus a $140,000 upgrade to a traceable mill. Kongwe risks losing two export contracts worth $1.9 million a year if it cannot prove sustainability.

questions.question_text: Define 'deforestation'.
questions.model_answer: Deforestation is the clearing or removal of forests and trees from land, usually so the land can be used for agriculture, logging, mining or settlement. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Clearing or removal of forests or trees
For agriculture, logging, mining or settlement

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why clearing native forest harms the environment.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Habitats and biodiversity are destroyed [k], as clearing 640 hectares of native forest in the last 4 years removes homes for wildlife and reduces species diversity [app]. Reason 2: Forests store carbon, so their removal worsens climate change [k], and clearing on this scale across the 2,600-hectare plantation adds to greenhouse gas emissions [app].

knowledge_max_2: Destroys habitats and reduces biodiversity
Releases stored carbon, worsening climate change
application_max_2: 640 hectares of native forest cleared in the last 4 years
Clearing across the 2,600-hectare plantation

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Kongwe of gaining sustainable palm oil certification.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Continued access to export markets [k], because buyers in Country Y now demand certified sustainable palm oil, and certification protects two export contracts worth $1.9 million a year [app], safeguarding the export revenue stream the business depends on [an]. Benefit 2: A stronger public image [k], as certification shows Kongwe takes environmental responsibility seriously after the Earthwatch Alliance report [app], attracting buyers who value sustainability and reducing the risk of consumer boycotts [an].

knowledge_max_2: Certification keeps export market access open
Certification improves public image and reputation
application_max_2: Country Y buyers now demand certified sustainable palm oil
Two export contracts worth $1.9 million a year at risk
analysis_max_2: Export revenue stream is safeguarded
Lower risk of boycotts from sustainability-minded buyers

questions.question_text: Do you think Kongwe should pay for sustainable palm oil certification? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for certification is that it secures the company's markets [k], protecting two export contracts worth $1.9 million a year by meeting Country Y buyers' demands, at a cost of $85,000 a year plus a $140,000 one-off mill upgrade [app], so annual certification fees absorb only about 4.5% of the protected revenue [an]. However, one argument against is the ongoing cost [k], since certification costs $85,000 a year indefinitely and $140,000 for traceable mills, reducing profit for a business earning $4.6 million in exports [app], and Kongwe could instead plant only on degraded land to rebuild trust without the audit burden [an]. Overall, Kongwe should pay for the certification [eval], because preserving $1.9 million of export contracts far outweighs $225,000 of first-year costs and protects its position in the 3,000 supermarket products that rely on its palm oil [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Certification secures export markets
Certification carries ongoing costs and audits
application_max_2: $85,000 a year plus $140,000 one-off mill upgrade; first year $225,000
Two export contracts worth $1.9 million a year at stake
analysis_max_2: Annual fees are only about 4.5% of protected revenue
Degraded-land replanting rebuilds trust without audit costs
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both certifying and avoiding certification costs
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Stonemill Precision Ltd is a maker of wind-turbine gearboxes based in the capital city of Country X. It wants to build a $6.5 million factory in Ravenfield, a former mining town where the last coal mine closed in 2019 after seven decades of coal extraction. The new plant would employ 240 workers at average wages of $34,000, with a further 110 jobs expected at local suppliers.

Ravenfield's unemployment rate is 13% and its high street has 27 empty shops. The government has offered a $900,000 training grant and 5 years without business rates if Stonemill proceeds. However, residents fear 600 lorry movements a week near the Ravenfield Levels, a protected wetland, and the board prefers expanding the existing site 120 kilometres away.

questions.question_text: Define 'external benefits'.
questions.model_answer: External benefits are the positive effects of a business activity that accrue to third parties not involved in the transaction, such as job creation, training opportunities and the regeneration of local areas. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Positive effects on third parties not involved in the activity
Examples include jobs, training and local regeneration

questions.question_text: Explain two external benefits the Stonemill factory would bring to Ravenfield.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: New jobs would cut unemployment [k], as 240 jobs at average wages of $34,000 plus 110 supplier jobs would lift a town with a 13% unemployment rate [app]. Reason 2: Skills and regeneration would improve [k], since the government's $900,000 training grant would raise local skills and spending would help revive 27 empty shops [app].

knowledge_max_2: Job creation reduces local unemployment
Training and regeneration raise local skills and spending
application_max_2: 240 jobs at average wages of $34,000 plus 110 supplier jobs
$900,000 training grant and 27 empty shops on the high street

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the government offers Stonemill a $900,000 training grant and 5 years without business rates.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To regenerate a deprived area [k], because Ravenfield's 13% unemployment and 27 empty shops show the town needs private investment after the coal mine closed in 2019 [app], so public money leverages far more private spending than it costs [an]. Reason 2: To build a skilled industrial workforce [k], as training 240 workers with a $900,000 grant creates transferable manufacturing skills [app], raising local productivity and helping attract further employers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Public money levers private investment and regeneration
Grants create transferable skills in the local workforce
application_max_2: Ravenfield has 13% unemployment and 27 empty shops after the 2019 mine closure
$900,000 grant to train 240 workers with 5 years free of business rates
analysis_max_2: Leveraged private spending exceeds the public cost
Skills raise productivity and attract further employers

questions.question_text: Do you think Stonemill Precision Ltd should build its new factory in Ravenfield? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for building in Ravenfield is the strong support package [k], with $900,000 of training grants and 5 years free of business rates cutting the cost of a $6.5 million project [app], while 240 jobs at $34,000 and 110 supplier jobs would transform a town with 13% unemployment [an]. However, one argument against is the environmental and logistical risk [k], as 600 lorry movements a week near the protected Ravenfield Levels could trigger legal action and delays [app], whereas expanding the capital site 120 kilometres away reuses existing infrastructure and avoids the wetland [an]. Overall, Stonemill Precision Ltd should build in Ravenfield [eval], because the public subsidy and available labour outweigh the traffic concerns, and routing lorries away from the Levels on agreed timetables would protect the wetland while keeping regeneration on track [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Support package cuts project costs
Environmental and logistical risks at the wetland site
application_max_2: $900,000 training grant and 5 years of waived business rates on a $6.5 million project
600 lorry movements a week near the Ravenfield Levels; 120 kilometres to capital site
analysis_max_2: Jobs and suppliers transform a 13% unemployment town
Capital site reuses infrastructure and avoids legal action
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both Ravenfield construction and capital-site expansion
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Thornwick Rail Freight Terminal is a private company in Country X transferring supermarket goods from lorries to rail. Last year it moved 84,000 containers of supermarket goods, employed 96 staff and had turnover of $12 million. The terminal operates around the clock beside the Marsh Meadow estate, home to 380 residents and a primary school.

Noise monitoring recorded 62 decibels at the nearest houses at night, and the council logged 48 complaints in 6 months from residents living closest to the rail line. The primary school reported disrupted lessons during 55 nightly shunting movements. Thornwick can spend $150,000 on acoustic barriers and silent track, ban shunting between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., cutting capacity by 18%, or pay compensation to Marsh Meadow residents.

questions.question_text: Define 'noise pollution'.
questions.model_answer: Noise pollution is unwanted or excessive sound that harms people's health and wellbeing, for example from lorries, machinery or trains operating near homes and schools. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Unwanted or excessive sound
Harms health and wellbeing of people nearby

questions.question_text: Explain two external costs created for Marsh Meadow residents by the terminal.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Lost sleep and stress from night noise [k], with 62 decibels recorded at the nearest houses, causing 48 complaints to the council in 6 months [app]. Reason 2: Disrupted learning for children [k], as 55 nightly shunting movements disturb lessons at the primary school serving the estate [app].

knowledge_max_2: Night noise causes lost sleep and stress
Noise disrupts nearby services such as schools
application_max_2: 62 decibels at the nearest houses; 48 complaints in 6 months
55 nightly shunting movements disrupting the primary school

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on Thornwick Rail Freight Terminal of banning shunting between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Lower night capacity [k], as the ban cuts capacity by 18%, reducing the containers moved from 84,000 a year [app], so supermarket contracts may be lost to rival terminals, cutting revenue [an]. Effect 2: Fewer complaints and legal risks [k], because removing the 55 nightly movements silences the loudest noise source for 380 residents [app], meaning fewer fines, better relations and goodwill for future expansion plans [an].

knowledge_max_2: Night ban reduces terminal capacity
Night ban removes the noise source and complaints
application_max_2: Ban would cut capacity by 18% from 84,000 containers a year
55 nightly shunting movements causing 48 complaints over 6 months
analysis_max_2: Lost contracts and revenue to rival terminals
Goodwill and fewer fines support future expansion

questions.question_text: Do you think Thornwick Rail Freight Terminal should spend $150,000 on acoustic barriers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for the barriers is that they fix the noise without reducing capacity [k], so the terminal keeps its 24-hour operation, 84,000 containers and $12 million turnover while protecting 380 residents and the primary school [app], preventing lost contracts and keeping the community willing to accept future expansion [an]. However, one argument against is that $150,000 is a direct cash cost [k], and the terminal could instead ban 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. shunting at no capital cost [app], though that cuts capacity by 18% and compensation to residents solves nothing if noise continues [an]. Overall, Thornwick Rail Freight Terminal should spend the $150,000 on acoustic barriers [eval], because they remove the 62-decibel night noise without sacrificing the 84,000-container business, protecting long-term revenue better than restricting hours or paying compensation [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Barriers remove noise while retaining capacity
Alternatives: night ban (free but capacity cut) or compensation (no noise reduction)
application_max_2: $150,000 cost versus 24-hour operation, 84,000 containers and $12 million turnover
10 p.m. to 6 a.m. ban would cut capacity by 18%; 62 decibels at nearest houses
analysis_max_2: Community goodwill supports future expansion
Compensation does not reduce the underlying noise
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both acoustic barriers and the night ban or compensation
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Brackenfeld Salmon Farm Ltd is a private limited company in Country X raising salmon in sea cages off Dunara Bay. It produces 1,700 tonnes a year, employs 44 staff and earns export revenue of $5.2 million. The same bay supports 60 local fishing boats and a small holiday-cottage sector popular with summer tourists.

The company proposes doubling output to 3,400 tonnes by installing 6 more cages, investing $2.8 million and creating 26 extra jobs. However, the Fishery Trust reports that waste feed and sea lice from the current cages have already cut wild fish numbers in the bay by 30%. The government will only licence new cages if farms meet a strict sustainability standard costing $120,000 a year, and the 26 extra jobs would mainly go to harbour workers in Dunara.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainable development'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainable development is meeting the needs of people today without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, balancing economic growth with environmental protection. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Meeting present needs without compromising future generations
Balancing economic growth with environmental protection

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Brackenfeld must weigh environmental effects before expanding.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The bay is already under pressure [k], because sea lice and waste feed from the current cages have reduced wild fish numbers by 30%, threatening the 60 local fishing boats [app]. Reason 2: The government controls further licences [k], since new cages are allowed only if farms meet a sustainability standard costing $120,000 a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Existing pollution already harms the bay ecosystem
Government licences require a sustainability standard
application_max_2: Wild fish numbers down 30%; 60 local fishing boats affected
Sustainability standard costing $120,000 a year required for new licences

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Brackenfeld if it must meet the sustainability standard.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Higher annual costs [k], as the sustainability standard costs $120,000 a year on top of the $2.8 million investment to double output to 3,400 tonnes [app], squeezing profit margins on exports worth $5.2 million [an]. Problem 2: Ongoing compliance burden [k], because feed sourcing, stocking density and water-quality monitoring must be maintained to keep the licence [app], risking fines or a refused licence if any check fails [an].

knowledge_max_2: Sustainability standard adds annual costs
Licence requires ongoing monitoring and audits

Feed sourcing, stocking density and water-quality monitoring needed

Failed checks risk fines or licence refusal

questions.question_text: Do you think Brackenfeld should double its salmon output? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for doubling output is the economic gain [k], as investing $2.8 million to reach 3,400 tonnes would create 26 extra jobs and lift exports beyond $5.2 million [app], benefiting the coastal town through wages, supplier spending and tax revenue [an]. However, one argument against is the environmental damage [k], since the bay has already seen a 30% decline in wild fish numbers, and installing 6 more cages would add more waste feed and sea lice [app], so the sustainability standard must be met or the expansion licence will be refused anyway [an]. Overall, Brackenfeld should expand only by meeting the sustainability standard [eval], because certified growth to 3,400 tonnes keeps the licence, protects the bay's wild fish and lets the community share the benefits without repeating the 30% decline [eval].

Expansion worsens pollution and requires the sustainability standard

Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Amberfield Brewery Ltd is a private limited company in Country X brewing 26,000 hectolitres of ale a year. It employs 58 staff and generates sales revenue of $7.1 million. Brewing produces 340 tonnes of spent grain and 9,000 cubic metres of wastewater annually.

Currently spent grain goes to landfill at a cost of $31,000 a year, and wastewater is piped to the town sewer serving 14,000 households for a charge of $46,000 a year. A recycling contractor will collect spent grain free of charge as animal feed, and an anaerobic digester would cut sewerage charges by 60% while producing biogas worth $38,000 a year. The brewery must invest $240,000 in tanks and pipes within the next 12 months, and landfill tax rises by 12% each year.

questions.question_text: Define 'recycling'.
questions.model_answer: Recycling is the process of converting waste materials into new products, reducing the need for raw materials, landfill space and pollution. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Converting waste materials into new products
Reduces use of raw materials, landfill and pollution

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the digester project would benefit Amberfield Brewery.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Lower sewerage charges [k], as the anaerobic digester would cut the $46,000 a year wastewater charge by 60% [app]. Reason 2: A new income stream from biogas [k], as the digester would produce gas worth $38,000 a year while landfill tax rises by 12% annually [app].

knowledge_max_2: Digester cuts sewerage charges
Digester produces biogas income
application_max_2: 60% cut in the $46,000 a year wastewater charge
Biogas worth $38,000 a year; landfill tax rising 12% each year

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why reducing brewery waste matters for the environment.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Less waste goes to landfill [k], as the 340 tonnes of spent grain the brewery sends to landfill each year take valuable space and produce methane, a powerful greenhouse gas [app], so diverting it to animal feed lowers the brewery's contribution to climate change [an]. Reason 2: Cleaner local rivers [k], because 9,000 cubic metres of wastewater a year can pollute waterways if it is released untreated [app], protecting fish and river life downstream of the brewery [an].

knowledge_max_2: Landfill releases methane, a greenhouse gas
Untreated wastewater pollutes waterways
application_max_2: 340 tonnes of spent grain sent to landfill each year
9,000 cubic metres of wastewater produced annually
analysis_max_2: Diverting grain to feed lowers climate change contribution
Protecting fish and river life downstream

questions.question_text: Do you think Amberfield Brewery should invest $240,000 in the digester project? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for the investment is the steady annual benefit [k], as the digester cuts the $46,000 sewerage charge by 60%, about $27,600 a year, and produces biogas worth $38,000 a year, together roughly $65,600 a year [app], while free collection of spent grain separately removes the $31,000 landfill cost [an]. However, one argument against is the upfront cost and complexity [k], as $240,000 is a major outlay for a business with $7.1 million revenue and 58 staff [app], and the tanks must be maintained and the 60% saving depends on the digester running reliably [an]. Overall, Amberfield Brewery should invest in the digester [eval], because roughly $65,600 a year of savings plus income recovers the $240,000 in under 4 years, ahead of landfill tax rising by 12% each year, while cutting pollution from 9,000 cubic metres of wastewater [eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Fairhaven Textiles Ltd is a private limited company in Country X weaving cotton fabrics for export. It employs 210 workers across two mills and produces 3.4 million metres of cloth a year for clothing retailers in 6 countries. Annual energy costs are $480,000, one fifth of total operating costs.

The board is considering rooftop solar panels and a biomass boiler costing $720,000. The system would cut grid electricity and gas purchases by 55%, saving $264,000 a year, but the cost would take almost 3 years to recover. The system would also improve energy security. Two German buyers have offered longer contracts if Fairhaven can show a 40% cut in carbon emissions, and the mills' boilers are 14 years old and due for replacement.

questions.question_text: Define 'renewable energy'.
questions.model_answer: Renewable energy comes from natural sources that are continuously replenished, such as solar, wind, hydroelectric and biomass power, unlike finite fossil fuels which will eventually run out. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Energy from natural sources that are continuously replenished
Examples include solar, wind, hydroelectric and biomass power

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the solar and biomass investment would benefit Fairhaven Textiles.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Lower energy bills [k], as cutting purchases by 55% saves $264,000 a year against current energy costs of $480,000 [app]. Reason 2: Access to longer export contracts [k], as two German buyers have offered longer contracts if Fairhaven shows a 40% cut in carbon emissions [app].

knowledge_max_2: Solar and biomass cut energy bills
Lower emissions unlock new or longer contracts
application_max_2: 55% cut saves $264,000 a year against $480,000 energy costs
Two German buyers offer longer contracts for a 40% emissions cut

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why environmentally responsible suppliers are attractive to buyers.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Lower risk of supply chain blame [k], as buyers face public pressure over the environmental impact of the products they sell, so Fairhaven's 40% emissions cut makes it a safer partner [app], reducing the risk of negative publicity for the German buyers [an]. Reason 2: Compliance with export market expectations [k], since two German buyers have already offered longer contracts to suppliers proving lower carbon emissions [app], making Fairhaven more competitive against suppliers who cannot demonstrate sustainability [an].

knowledge_max_2: Buyers manage reputational risk in their supply chains
Export markets increasingly require proven low emissions
application_max_2: Fairhaven's planned 40% emissions cut
Two German buyers offering longer contracts for proven cuts
analysis_max_2: Negative publicity risk for buyers is reduced
Sustainability proof makes Fairhaven more competitive

questions.question_text: Do you think Fairhaven Textiles should install the solar panels and biomass boiler? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for installing the system is the long-term saving [k], as $264,000 a year off a $480,000 energy bill, together with replacing 14-year-old boilers, means the $720,000 cost recovers in almost 3 years [app], after which savings flow straight to profit while emissions fall 40% [an]. However, one argument against is the heavy upfront cost [k], since $720,000 must be found now, reducing cash available for wages to 210 workers and other investment [app], and the savings depend on sunlight and biomass supply, which vary between the two mills [an]. Overall, Fairhaven Textiles should install the solar panels and biomass boiler [eval], because two German buyers' longer contracts and the 40% emissions cut protect its export future, and recovering $720,000 in under 3 years makes the project financially sound as well as sustainable [eval].

knowledge_max_2: System recovers its cost through annual savings
Heavy upfront cost competes with other spending
application_max_2: $264,000 a year saving recovers $720,000 in almost 3 years
40% emissions cut unlocks two German buyers' longer contracts
analysis_max_2: Savings after recovery flow straight to profit
Savings vary with sunlight and biomass supply between the two mills
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both installing the system and its upfront cost or risks
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Hartham Ridge Wind Farm Ltd is a new company formed to build an 8-turbine wind farm costing $14 million on high moorland in Country X. The site would generate 21 megawatts, enough for 11,000 homes, and create 34 construction jobs plus 9 permanent maintenance roles over 14 months of building.

The moorland lies 3 kilometres from Hartham village, home to 620 residents, and 900 metres from a popular walking trail. Hartham Ridge Action, a local environmental pressure group, gathered 700 signatures against the farm, and 45% of residents oppose it, citing noise of about 38 decibels and visual impact. The council will consent only if the company funds a $120,000-a-year community benefit scheme and shuts 2 turbines during bird migration, cutting output by 9%.

questions.question_text: Define 'environmental pressure group'.
questions.model_answer: An environmental pressure group is an organisation that campaigns to influence business and government decisions to protect the natural environment, using publicity, petitions and lobbying. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Organisation campaigning to protect the environment
Uses publicity, petitions and lobbying to influence decisions

questions.question_text: Explain two external benefits the wind farm would bring to Country X.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Clean electricity for homes [k], as the 8 turbines would generate 21 megawatts, enough to power 11,000 homes without burning fossil fuels [app]. Reason 2: Jobs for the local area [k], as 34 construction jobs and 9 permanent maintenance roles would be created over 14 months of building [app].

knowledge_max_2: Wind farms generate clean electricity without fossil fuels
Wind farms create jobs for local people
application_max_2: 21 megawatts, enough for 11,000 homes
34 construction jobs plus 9 permanent roles over 14 months

questions.question_text: Explain two external costs the Hartham Ridge wind farm may create.
questions.model_answer: Cost 1: Noise disturbance for villagers [k], since Hartham village, 3 kilometres away with 620 residents, faces turbine noise of about 38 decibels [app], which may disturb sleep and reduce house prices, costs falling on people who gain no direct electricity [an]. Cost 2: Harm to wildlife and the landscape [k], as shutting 2 turbines during bird migration shows a real collision risk, and the moorland skyline is a valued landscape [app], damaging a recreational asset used by walkers on the nearby trail [an].

knowledge_max_2: Turbines create noise affecting nearby residents
Wind farms affect wildlife and valued landscapes
application_max_2: Hartham village 3 kilometres away, 620 residents, noise of about 38 decibels
2 turbines shut during bird migration; 900-metre-away walking trail
analysis_max_2: Sleep disturbance and lower house prices for residents
Damage to a recreational and ecological asset

questions.question_text: Do you think Hartham Ridge Wind Farm Ltd should proceed under the council's conditions? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for proceeding is the clean energy and jobs [k], as 21 megawatts would supply 11,000 homes while 34 construction jobs and 9 permanent roles are created [app], giving Country X lower-carbon electricity and lasting employment on the moorland [an]. However, one argument against is the impact on Hartham [k], since 45% of 620 residents oppose the farm over noise of about 38 decibels and visual impact on the valued skyline [app], and the $120,000-a-year community fund plus a 9% output cut from shutting 2 turbines eat into returns on the $14 million project [an]. Overall, Hartham Ridge Wind Farm Ltd should proceed under the council's conditions [eval], because clean power for 11,000 homes and 43 jobs outweigh the residual disruption, and the community fund plus migration shutdowns fairly compensate Hartham while keeping the wind farm viable [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Proceeding delivers clean energy and jobs
Resident opposition and compliance conditions erode returns
application_max_2: 21 megawatts for 11,000 homes; 34 construction and 9 permanent jobs
$120,000-a-year community fund; 9% output cut from 2 turbines; $14 million cost
analysis_max_2: Lower-carbon electricity and lasting local employment
Compliance conditions reduce returns on the $14 million project
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both proceeding under conditions and resident opposition
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures
